newsitem.title: USA: United HealthCare sees 20 pct EPS growth.
newsitem.headline: United HealthCare sees 20 pct EPS growth.

text.p: United HealthCare Corp said Wednesday it expects earnings per share to increase at least 20 percent annually in the next few years, as premium growth exceeds medical cost increases.

"Twenty percent or more in growth in earnings per share (annually) is a good target for us," chairman and chief executive William McGuire told reporters following the company's annual shareholder meeting.
"We believe we can grow that much sequentially in the next several years," he said.
According to First Call, analysts expect on average a 22 percent increase in earnings per share, to $2.39 a share for 1997 versus $1.96 last year.
McGuire said he expects premium revenues to begin to increase faster than medical costs sometime during 1997.

"We assume that the premium revenues will increase faster than medical costs this year, but it's too early to know if it'll be for the whole year," McGuire said. "Our objective is to get them in parallel with each other."

Longer term, McGuire said the company will strive to attain a medical cost ratio of 82 percent, but said reaching 80 percent would be difficult. The medical cost ratio is the percent of premiums used to pay medical costs.
"Our job is to ensure people pay the right price for the quality healthcare product," McGuire said. "And if that means the medical cost ratio is 82 percent, then that's fine."
In the first quarter 1997, United HealthCare had a medical cost ratio of 84.4 percent, in 1996 84.6 percent and in 1995 79.7 percent.
McGuire said the company is likely to post total 1998 revenues between $17 billion and $18 billion.

"The forecast would put us at $17 to $18 billion (in revenues in 1998) when you bring in AARP (American Association of Retired Persons)," he said. "You might have 15 to 20 percent top line growth on an existing basis, and then you bring in AARP in 1998. We will probably get there."
The company had $10.034 billion in total revenues in 1996 and McGuire said the company has $3.8 billion in "locked-in business" when it begins coverage for 4.8 million AARP members in January 1998.
